description: We're LunaZen: space-exploration and technology enthusiasts who love applied science and maths. We're tackling the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, comparing south-pole landing sites by Sun and Earth visibility over real terrain. Join us if you enjoy space, data or design, and want to help make lunar mission planning clearer for everyone.
summary:
LunaZen transforms lunar terrain data into fast, actionable mission-planning intelligence while making lunar science accessible to everyone.

We developed an interactive, browser-based Lunar Landing Site Navigator that goes beyond conventional illumination maps. Using NASA datasets, SPICE-based geometry and multi-resolution terrain modelling, LunaZen calculates when both the Sun and Earth are visible above the actual lunar terrain horizon.

For mission planners, it evaluates mission windows, landing dispersion and prolonged darkness, with interactive what-if analysis to explore alternative landing sites, arrival dates and mission constraints. Its responsive interface delivers planning results almost instantly.

Under the hood, advanced terrain-horizon ray tracing, lunar-curvature modelling and extended-disk visibility calculations are integrated into a dual Python–JavaScript scientific engine.

For educators, students and the public, the same scientific engine provides intuitive maps, interactive terrain visualisations, panoramas and 3D views that bring the lunar south pole to life.

LunaZen bridges scientific rigour, practical mission planning and accessible lunar exploration, helping users not just see the Moon, but understand what it takes to land and operate there.
details:
LunaZen: From Lunar Terrain to Mission Decisions

Overview video (3 min): https://youtu.be/9aBHnTUXZ4o

GitHub: https://github.com/lunazen-spaceapp/lunazen-v1

1. What we built

LunaZen is an interactive, browser-based Lunar Landing Site Navigator that combines scientific modelling, terrain visualisation and mission-planning capabilities in one platform.

Rather than relying solely on regional illumination maps, LunaZen models the actual terrain surrounding a landing location to determine when the Sun and Earth are visible above the local horizon. It transforms complex lunar geometry into actionable information for exploring landing sites and evaluating mission scenarios.

2. How it works: The science and technology

LunaZen brings together several computational techniques:

  • Astronomical geometry: Uses NASA/JPL SPICE kernels and planetary ephemerides to calculate the time-dependent positions and apparent geometry of the Sun, Earth and Moon, including light-time and stellar-aberration corrections.
  • Multi-resolution terrain modelling: Combines high-resolution local elevation data with broader lunar terrain models. Terrain-horizon ray tracing accounts for lunar curvature and identifies obstructions along the observer's line of sight.
  • Extended-body visibility: Unlike simple point-source calculations, LunaZen considers the apparent angular size of the Sun and Earth to determine how much of each disk is visible above the terrain skyline.
  • Mission analysis: Evaluates sunlight, darkness and Earth visibility over complete mission windows, including landing dispersion and the longest periods without sunlight or geometric communications visibility.

The application has a dual-engine architecture: a Python scientific reference implementation and a JavaScript browser engine. The two are tested against each other, allowing sophisticated scientific calculations to run interactively without requiring specialist software installations.

3. What users can do

LunaZen goes beyond displaying scientific data. It helps users investigate and make decisions through several integrated capabilities:

  • Planner: Evaluate landing opportunities against mission constraints, including landing dispersion, darkness tolerance and Earth visibility.
  • Constraint Relaxation: Explore what needs to change when a proposed landing scenario is infeasible.
  • Delay Analyzer: Examine the consequences of mission delays and identify subsequent feasible windows.
  • Compare Landings: Compare alternative locations and assess the impact of shifting landing dates.
  • Explorer: Simulate the changing positions of the Sun and Earth over time, using 15-minute time steps, and visualise them against actual local terrain horizons through interactive panoramas and 3D views. Explore time-dependent sunlight and Earth visibility, supported by visibility timelines and adjustable observer parameters.
  • Map and Rank: Explore and compare 13 candidate sites and 67 landing spots, alongside NASA illumination and Earth-visibility information. Users can also save custom spots within candidate landing sites and access these saved locations directly in Explorer and Planning for further visualisation and mission analysis.

The Planner can return results almost instantly, making it practical to explore multiple scenarios interactively.

4. What makes LunaZen different

The central innovation is the integration of terrain-aware scientific calculations with mission-level decision support.

A location that looks favourable on a regional illumination map may still have its sunlight or Earth visibility obstructed by local terrain. LunaZen addresses this by modelling the actual horizon and evaluating visibility over time.

More importantly, it does not stop at identifying a problem. Its interactive what-if capabilities allow users to investigate alternative landing sites, arrival dates, landing radii and darkness tolerances.

This bridges the gap between identifying a promising landing location and understanding whether a mission scenario can work there.

5. Validation and scientific credibility

Scientific reliability was a core design consideration. LunaZen includes an independent validation framework using reference data and observations that are separate from its own calculations.

The project's documented validation results include:

  • Sun and Earth directions matching JPL Horizons to 0.1 arcseconds across four sites and 70 dates per site.
  • 18.6-year average sunlight estimates matching NASA LOLA maps to 1.6 percentage points RMS across 26 locations.
  • Reproduction of seven Connecting Ridge regions reported by Barker et al. (2021) within 1.4 percentage points.
  • Apollo 11, 12 and 14 moonwalk Sun angles matching the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal to 0.12 degrees.
  • Reproduction of the Blue Ghost 1 sunset to approximately six minutes.

The browser-based calculations are also tested against the Python reference implementation.

6. Who benefits and why it matters

LunaZen is designed to serve multiple audiences through the same scientific engine:

  • Mission planners and researchers: Explore terrain-dependent visibility, assess landing windows and investigate alternative mission scenarios.
  • Educators and students: Understand lunar geometry, terrain horizons, illumination and communications through interactive scientific visualisations.
  • The general public: Explore the lunar south pole and experience the challenges of lunar landing without needing specialist scientific software.

By combining technical depth with an intuitive interface, LunaZen makes sophisticated lunar science both useful for analysis and accessible for learning.

7. Technology stack and development

The project uses Python for the scientific reference engine and data-processing workflows, and JavaScript for the interactive browser application. NASA/JPL SPICE kernels, lunar elevation models and scientific reference datasets provide the foundation for its calculations.

The application integrates scientific computation, geospatial processing, interactive maps, terrain visualisation and 3D rendering into a browser-based experience.

Development was human-directed and AI-assisted. Anthropic Claude and Claude Code supported software development and Python code generation. Manim, Kokoro and Microsoft Edge TTS were used in the video and audio production. The team directed the scientific approach, architectural decisions, implementation, validation and integration.

8. Impact and future potential

Lunar exploration will require increasingly sophisticated decisions about where to land, when to arrive and how to operate in challenging terrain and illumination conditions.

LunaZen provides an accessible framework for investigating these questions using real lunar data and physically grounded calculations. Its combination of scientific modelling, rapid scenario analysis and visual learning has potential beyond the immediate challenge: supporting education, public engagement and early-stage exploration of future lunar mission scenarios.

LunaZen makes the complex science of landing on the Moon something people can not only understand, but interact with.
